claim: Cryo-electron tomography (cryoET) has become a powerful technique at the interface of structural biology and cell biology due to its unique ability for imaging cells in their native state and determining structures of macromolecular complexes in their cellular context.
source: Cryo-electron tomography (cryoET) has become a powerful technique at the interface of structural biology and cell biology, due to its unique ability for imaging cells in their native state and determining structures of macromolecular complexes in their cellular context.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about cryoET capabilities and is referenced in the introduction with citations to Beck and Baumeister, 2016; Koning et al., 2018; Kooger et al., 2018; Oikonomou and Jensen, 2017; Plitzko et al., 2017.

claim: A limitation of cryoET is its restriction to relatively thin samples.
source: A limitation of cryoET is its restriction to relatively thin samples.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation in the abstract and is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: CryoET is restricted to samples that are well below 800 nm in thickness.
source: Unfortunately, cryoET is restricted to samples that are well below 800 nm in thickness, and requires sample thinning techniques for specimens like mammalian cells, C. elegans, yeast, cyanobacteria and biofilms.
evidence: This is a specific technical specification stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge about cryoET limitations.

claim: Sample thinning by cryo-focused ion beam (cryoFIB) milling has significantly expanded the range of samples that can be analyzed by cryoET.
source: Sample thinning by cryo-focused ion beam (cryoFIB) milling has significantly expanded the range of samples that can be analyzed by cryoET.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating the application of cryoFIB milling (Marko et al., 2007; Rigort et al., 2010).

claim: CryoFIB milling is low-throughput, time-consuming and manual.
source: Unfortunately, cryoFIB milling is low-throughput, time-consuming and manual.
evidence: This is stated as a problem motivating the study and is supported by the description of current manual workflows in the introduction.

claim: Biological cryoFIB milling uses a gallium ion beam to ablate segments of the sample in order to generate thin lamellae that can be imaged by cryoET.
source: Biological cryoFIB milling is an emerging sample thinning technique, which uses a gallium ion beam to ablate segments of the sample in order to generate thin lamellae that can be imaged by cryoET (Marko et al., 2007; Rigort et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a technical description of the cryoFIB milling method supported by citations.

claim: CryoFIB milling produces specimens without observable artifacts, in which in situ structural information is preserved.
source: Unlike previous methodologies, cryoFIB milling produces specimens without observable artifacts, in which in situ structural information is preserved.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about cryoFIB milling advantages and is contrasted with previous methodologies.

claim: CryoFIB milling has provided important insights into the cellular mechanisms of organisms too thick for direct imaging.
source: To date, its use has provided important insights into the cellular mechanisms of organisms too thick for direct imaging (e.g. Ader et al., 2019; Albert et al., 2017; Böck et al., 2017; Bykov et al., 2017; Cai et al., 2018; Chaikeeratisak et al., 2019; Delarue et al., 2018; Khanna et al., 2019; Mahamid et al., 2019; Mahamid et al., 2016; Rast et al., 2019; Swulius et al., 2018; Weiss et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to published studies demonstrating the application of cryoFIB milling.

claim: Up to 16 lamellae can be generated in a 10 hr session using current manual cryoFIB milling methods.
source: Using this method, up to 16 lamellae can be generated in a 10 hr session (Medeiros et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Medeiros et al., 2018.

claim: Current manual cryoFIB milling procedures require constant attention from the operator, including manual inputs every 5–15 min.
source: However, for such a session, the procedure requires constant attention from the operator. This includes, visually monitoring milling and providing manual inputs every 5–15 min, for example to execute a series of repetitive tasks such as target identification, positioning milling patterns, changing FIB currents, monitoring drift and visually determining milling end points.
evidence: This is a description of the current manual workflow based on established practice in the field.

claim: The automated sequential FIB milling method was implemented on two separate Zeiss Crossbeam 550 FIB-SEM instruments.
source: Automation was implemented on two separate Zeiss Crossbeam 550 FIB-SEM instruments, using routines that are available in the SmartFIB software package (Zeiss Microscopy GmbH, Oberkochen, Germany).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental setup and equipment used in the study.

claim: Stage backlash and drift correction modules are critical for reliable targeting of lamella preparation sites.
source: Particularly important are the modules for stage backlash and drift correction, which are critical for reliable targeting of lamella preparation sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' experience implementing the automated method.

claim: The automated method allows the user to set up all milling targets and then execute milling in an unattended, fully automated manner.
source: This allows the user to set up all milling targets and then execute milling in an unattended, fully automated manner.
evidence: This is a description of the capability of the developed method.

claim: The setup process for automated sequential milling takes approximately 9 min per target.
source: This setup process takes ~9 min per target.
evidence: This is a measured time value from the experimental implementation of the method.

claim: The automated sequential milling method was tested on Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain SK1 and Anabaena sp. PCC 7120 in nine independent milling sessions.
source: During the development of this method, we tested automated sequential milling on two separate Zeiss Crossbeam 550 instruments using the model organisms Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain SK1 (hereafter 'yeast') and the multicellular cyanobacteria Anabaena sp. PCC 7120 (hereafter 'cyanobacteria') in nine independent milling sessions (sessions A-I, Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design and samples used.

claim: Rough milling success rate was 98% (n = 123).
source: Rough milling success, as defined by the presence of an intact lamella at the targeted location after rough milling, was 98% (n = 123).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data presented in Table 1.

claim: The only failures in lamellae production were the result of user error.
source: The only failures in lamellae production were the result of user error, when rough milling was accidentally executed on the same target twice and on a grid bar (session F and I, respectively).
evidence: This is an analysis of the failure modes observed in the experimental data.

claim: The method successfully generated 10 lamellae spread across two grids containing two different samples in sessions B.1 and B.2.
source: With sessions B.1 and B.2, we also demonstrated the robustness of the targeting routine by successfully generating 10 lamellae spread across two grids containing two different samples (Table 1).
evidence: This is a specific experimental result demonstrating the method's capability.

claim: The success rate of automated sequential polishing was 88% (n = 106 rough lamellae).
source: In total, the success rate (intact lamella detected after polishing) of automated sequential polishing was 88% (n = 106 rough lamellae).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data presented in Table 1.

claim: 9 of the 13 failed polishing attempts occurred in session C in which the rough-milled lamellae were left in the FIB-SEM instrument for 10 hr before beginning automated polishing.
source: Importantly, 9 of the 13 failed polishing attempts occurred in session C in which the rough-milled lamellae were left in the FIB-SEM instrument for 10 hr before beginning automated polishing.
evidence: This is an analysis of the experimental data identifying a specific cause of failures.

claim: Rough lamellae left in the instrument for 10 hr before polishing showed signs of bending, which likely resulted in failure in lamellae polishing.
source: Prior to polishing, these rough lamellae showed signs of bending, which likely resulted in failure in lamellae polishing.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of the lamellae and correlation with polishing failures.

claim: When session C was repeated without a delay between rough milling and polishing (sessions H and I), bending was not observed and 95% polishing success was obtained.
source: In fact, when we repeated session C without a delay between rough milling and polishing (sessions H and I), we did not observe bending and obtained 95% polishing success.
evidence: This is experimental data from repeated experiments testing the effect of timing on polishing success.

claim: Of the lamellae generated in a fully automated manner (n = 93), 16% were lost in transfer and 3% exhibited contamination or cracks prohibiting data collection.
source: Of the lamellae that were generated in a fully automated manner (n = 93), 16% were lost in transfer and 3% exhibited contamination or cracks prohibiting data collection.
evidence: This is quantitative data about lamella quality and handling losses.

claim: Lamellae thicknesses ranged from 117 to 379 nm when final polishing patterns are placed 300 nm apart.
source: From the collected tomograms, we determined the lamellae thicknesses to range from 117 to 379 nm when final polishing patterns are placed 300 nm apart (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is measured data from tomograms, with supporting figures showing the distribution.

claim: The average thickness of lamellae generated in a fully automated manner (session B.2-I; 243 nm) is comparable to the thickness of manually polished lamellae (session A/B.1; 258 nm).
source: The average thickness of lamellae generated in a fully automated manner (session B.2-I; 243 nm) is comparable to the thickness of manually polished lamellae (session A/B.1; 258 nm).
evidence: This is a comparison of measured data between automated and manual methods.

claim: Yeast tomograms contained nuclei, nuclear pore complexes, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticula, cytoplasmic ribosomes and vacuoles.
source: Yeast tomograms contained nuclei, nuclear pore complexes, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticula, cytoplasmic ribosomes and vacuoles.
evidence: This is an observation from the tomographic data collected on yeast lamellae.

claim: Microtubules inside the nucleus were observed in one yeast tomogram and the number of protofilaments could be determined without averaging.
source: In one particular tomogram (Figure 3B/C), we observed microtubules inside the nucleus and were able to determine the number of protofilaments without averaging.
evidence: This is a specific observation from tomographic data with supporting images in Figure 3B/C.

claim: Cyanobacterial tomograms showed thylakoid membranes, phycobilisomes and septal junctions.
source: Cyanobacterial tomograms showed thylakoid membranes, phycobilisomes and septal junctions (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an observation from the tomographic data collected on cyanobacterial lamellae, with supporting image.

claim: From nine lamellae, a total of 412 subvolumes of cyanobacterial septal junctions were extracted, averaged and classified.
source: From nine lamellae, a total of 412 subvolumes were extracted, averaged and classified in order to remove misaligned particles.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing workflow with specific numbers.

claim: 343 subvolumes remained after classification and were averaged and symmetrized.
source: The 343 remaining subvolumes were then averaged and symmetrized.
evidence: This is a description of the final dataset used for averaging.

claim: The resulting structure of cyanobacterial septal junctions had the same architecture as previously described, including a cap module with five arches, a plug module and a tube module.
source: The resulting structure had the same architecture as previously described, including a cap module with five arches, a plug module and a tube module (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a comparison of the obtained structure with previously published results, supported by Figure 3F.

claim: Fourier shell correlation (FSC) analyses indicate that the average had a resolution that is similar to a structure calculated using the same number of particles extracted from tomograms generated by manual milling.
source: Fourier shell correlation (FSC) analyses indicate that the average had a resolution that is similar to a structure that was calculated using the same number of particles extracted from tomograms generated in a previous study by manual milling (Weiss et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of resolution between automated and manual methods, with supporting FSC curve in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The time investment by the operator is significantly reduced from approximately 10 hr in a manual milling session to approximately 2.4 hr for an automated sequential milling session, assuming 16 targets are milled.
source: First, the time investment by the operator is significantly reduced from ~10 hr in a manual milling session to ~2.4 hr for an automated sequential milling session, assuming 16 targets are milled.
evidence: This is a comparison of time requirements based on the experimental implementation of the method.

claim: The minimum required machine time is reduced from 30 to 45 min per lamella (manual method) to approximately 25.75 min per lamella (automated method).
source: Second, by removing the need for frequent user inputs and idle times, the minimum required machine time is reduced from 30 to 45 min (Medeiros et al., 2018) (i.e. 16 lamellae in 10 hr) to ~25.75 min (~9 min setup plus ~16.75 min milling) per lamella.
evidence: This is a calculated comparison of machine time efficiency between manual and automated methods, with citation to manual method timing.

claim: The automated procedure can be adapted to a wide range of samples and milling techniques.
source: Third, based on the robustness and customizable nature of the method, the procedure can be adapted to a wide range of samples and milling techniques (Toro-Nahuelpan et al., 2020; Wolff et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference about the method's applicability based on its design features, with citations to other milling techniques.

claim: The automated procedure will allow the user to systematically explore novel milling methods by reusing uniform milling patterns.
source: Fourth, the automated procedure will allow the user to systematically explore novel milling methods by reusing uniform milling patterns.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of the method.

claim: The method can be combined with correlated approaches that allow for target pre-screening, for instance cryo-light microscopy or cryo-FIB-SEM volume imaging.
source: Fifth, the method can generally be combined with correlated approaches that allow for target pre-screening, for instance cryo-light microscopy or cryo-FIB-SEM volume imaging (Eibauer et al., 2012; Gorelick et al., 2019; Koning et al., 2014; Schertel et al., 2013; Schorb et al., 2017; Sviben et al., 2016; Vidavsky et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the method's compatibility with other techniques, supported by citations to correlated imaging approaches.

claim: The development of automated sequential cryoFIB milling renders cryoET applicable to previously unfeasible projects.
source: Altogether, the development of automated sequential cryoFIB milling renders cryoET applicable to previously unfeasible projects.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated improvements in throughput and efficiency.

claim: The method was established and tested on two different Crossbeam 550 FIB-SEM instruments equipped with copper band-cooled mechanical cryo-stages and integrated VCT500 vacuum transfer systems.
source: The method was established and tested on two different Crossbeam 550 FIB-SEM instruments (Carl Zeiss Microscopy) equipped with copper band-cooled mechanical cryo-stages and integrated VCT500 vacuum transfer systems (Leica Microsystems).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental equipment used.

claim: Samples were sputter-coated with a ~4 nm thick layer of tungsten under cryogenic conditions.
source: Under cryogenic conditions the plunge-frozen sample were sputter-coated with a ~4 nm thick layer of tungsten.
evidence: This is a description of the sample preparation protocol.

claim: The gas injection system (GIS) was used to deposit an organometallic platinum precursor layer onto each grid.
source: In the Crossbeam 550, the gas injection system (GIS) was used to deposit an organometallic platinum precursor layer onto each grid.
evidence: This is a description of the sample preparation protocol.

claim: To enhance conductivity and decrease the effects of charging, the plunge-frozen sample was coated with a ~4 nm layer of tungsten.
source: To enhance conductivity and decrease the effects of charging, the plunge-frozen sample was coated with a ~4 nm layer of tungsten.
evidence: This is a description of the purpose and method of tungsten coating.

claim: A protection layer of organometallic platinum precursor was deposited onto each grid to minimize the effects of curtaining.
source: After inserting the holder into the FIB-SEM, a protection layer of organometallic platinum precursor was deposited onto each grid to minimize the effects of curtaining.
evidence: This is a description of the purpose and method of platinum deposition.

claim: For deposition under cryo-conditions, it is essential that the heating element of the GIS needle and reservoir are turned off to keep the system at room temperature (28°C).
source: For deposition under cryo-conditions, it is essential that the heating element of the GIS needle and reservoir are turned off to keep the system at room temperature (28°C).
evidence: This is a technical detail about the protocol based on experimental optimization.

claim: Backlash correction was included for all automated stage movements.
source: In addition, backlash correction was also included for all automated stage movements, using the user preference settings of the software SmartSEM (Carl Zeiss Microscopy).
evidence: This is a description of a key feature of the automated method.

claim: For cryo-TEM lamella preparation, the material 'vitrified ice' was created using a dose calibration of 20 mC/cm² being equivalent to a milling depth of 1 µm in cross-section mode.
source: For cryo-TEM lamella preparation, the material 'vitrified ice' was created using a dose calibration of 20 mC/cm² being equivalent to a milling depth of 1 µm in cross-section mode.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the milling calibration used.

claim: During automated sequential milling a total of four currents were used for rough milling (700, 300 and 100 pA) and polishing (50 pA).
source: During automated sequential milling a total of four currents were used for rough milling (700 pA, 300 pA and 100 pA) and polishing (50 pA).
evidence: This is a description of the milling parameters used in the protocol.

claim: Exposure of a typical rough milling target took about 12 min.
source: Exposure of a typical rough milling target took about 12 min.
evidence: This is a measured time value from the experimental implementation.

claim: Polishing typically took about 4.75 min.
source: Polishing typically took about 4.75 min.
evidence: This is a measured time value from the experimental implementation.

claim: Instrument 2 suffered from stage drift, which caused issues during polishing.
source: Note that instrument 2 (Table 1) suffered from stage drift, which caused issues during polishing.
evidence: This is an observation about instrument-specific issues encountered during experiments.

claim: A wait time of 3 min was applied to allow the stage to settle before polishing on instrument 2.
source: Unfortunately, SmartFIB does not have an integrated wait time, however, using a set of low current (1–5 pA) patterns, we were able to apply a wait time of 3 min to allow the stage to settle before polishing.
evidence: This is a description of a workaround implemented to address stage drift issues.

claim: Data was collected on a Titan Krios 300kV electron microscope equipped with a field emission gun, imaging filter (slit width 20 eV) and K2 or K3 direct electron detector.
source: Data was collected on a Titan Krios 300kV electron microscope (ThermoFisher) equipped with a field emission gun, imaging filter (Gatan, Pleasanton, U.S.) (slit width 20 eV) and K2 or K3 direct electron detector (Gatan).
evidence: This is a description of the equipment used for data collection.

claim: Cyanobacteria data was collected at 2° increments between +60° and −60° with a defocus of −8 µm, total accumulated dose of ~140 e- / Å2 and pixel size of 3.38 Å.
source: Cyanobacteria data was collected with UCSF Tomo (Zheng et al., 2007) at 2° increments between +60° and −60°. Data was collected at a defocus of −8 µm, total accumulated dose of ~140 e- / Å2 and pixel size of 3.38 Å.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection parameters for cyanobacteria samples.

claim: Yeast tomograms were collected at 2° increments between +60° and −60° with a defocus of −8 µm, total accumulated dose of ~120 e- / Å2 and pixel size of 4.57 Å.
source: Yeast tomograms were collected using SerialEM between +60° and −60° at 2° increments with a defocus of −8 µm, total accumulated dose of ~120 e- / Å2 and pixel size of 4.57 Å.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection parameters for yeast samples.

claim: Tomogram reconstruction and subtomogram averaging was performed according to Weiss et al. (2019).
source: Tomogram reconstruction and subtomogram averaging was performed according to Weiss et al. (2019).
evidence: This is a reference to the methods used for data processing.

claim: Tomograms were reconstructed using the IMOD package.
source: Briefly, tomograms were reconstructed using the IMOD package (Kremer et al., 1996) and septal junction subtomogram averaging was performed using PEET (Nicastro et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a description of the software used for tomogram reconstruction with citation.

claim: Septal junction subtomogram averaging was performed using PEET.
source: Briefly, tomograms were reconstructed using the IMOD package (Kremer et al., 1996) and septal junction subtomogram averaging was performed using PEET (Nicastro et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a description of the software used for subtomogram averaging with citation.

claim: 412 particles were extracted and averaged in a box of 44 × 44 × 44 pixels with a pixel size of 6.8 Å.
source: A total of 412 particles were extracted and averaged in a box of 44 × 44 × 44 pixels with a pixel size of 6.8 Å.
evidence: This is a description of the subtomogram averaging parameters.

claim: PEET classification was used to remove misaligned particles, resulting in 343 final particles.
source: PEET classification was then used to remove misaligned particles (343 final particles).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing workflow.

claim: 5-fold symmetry was applied to obtain the final average.
source: 5-fold symmetry was applied to obtain the final average.
evidence: This is a description of the symmetry applied in the averaging process.

claim: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae SK1 strain used in this study is diploid, homozygous for ndt80∆::HIS3 ho::LYS2 ura3 leu2::hisG trp1::hisG his3::hisG.
source: diploid, homozygous for ndt80∆::HIS3 ho::LYS2 ura3 leu2::hisG trp1::hisG his3::hisG
evidence: This is the genotype information provided in Table 2.

claim: The Anabaena sp. PCC7120 strain used in this study is wild type.
source: Wild Type
evidence: This is the genotype information provided in Table 2.

claim: The cyanobacterial cell line originates from Rippka et al. (1979).
source: The cyanobacterial cell line originates from Rippka et al. (1979).
evidence: This is a citation providing the source of the strain.

claim: The yeast strain was generated in this study.
source: The yeast strain was generated in this study.
evidence: This is a statement about the origin of the yeast strain used.

claim: Grids were back-blotted twice for 3–5 s each time, at 4°C with 95% humidity and plunged into liquid ethane/propane using a Vitrobot.
source: Grids were back-blotted twice for 3–5 s each time, at 4°C with 95% humidity and plunged into liquid ethane/propane using a Vitrobot (ThermoFisher).
evidence: This is a description of the plunge-freezing protocol.

claim: FIB current alignments between different currents at a given voltage (30 kV for biological cryo-samples) should be checked and optimized.
source: While the SEM column alignments are stable and non-essential during automated milling, the FIB alignment between different currents at a given voltage (30 kV for biological cryo-samples) should be checked and optimized.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental protocol development.

claim: FIB calibration is typically done weekly or when deemed necessary and takes roughly 60 min to complete.
source: Typically, this calibration is done weekly or when deemed necessary and takes roughly 60 min to complete.
evidence: This is a description of the calibration schedule and time requirement.

claim: Standard FIB calibration procedures are best performed on a silicon wafer due to its structural homogeneity, which allows better evaluation of the FIB beam shape.
source: In case of deviation, on-the-fly adjustments are possible on a loaded cryo-sample, however, standard calibration procedures are best performed on a silicon wafer due to its structural homogeneity, which allows better evaluation of the FIB beam shape.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on practical considerations for calibration.

claim: When the FIB current is properly calibrated, the beam will produce a spot that is round with sharp edges.
source: When the current is properly calibrated, the beam will produce a spot that is round with sharp edges.
evidence: This is a description of the expected outcome of proper calibration.

claim: For cold deposition of platinum precursor, the holder was moved 3 mm below the coincidence point and tilted to 20°.
source: For cold deposition of platinum precursor, the holder was moved 3 mm below the coincidence point and tilted to 20°.
evidence: This is a description of the protocol for platinum deposition.

claim: By positioning the GIS needle above each grid and opening the GIS for 45 s, a layer of platinum precursor was deposited onto the sample.
source: By positioning the GIS needle above each grid and opening the GIS for 45 s, a layer of platinum precursor was deposited onto the sample.
evidence: This is a description of the platinum deposition protocol.

claim: Since the GIS needle was mounted at a similar angle as the FIB column, deposition of platinum occurred preferentially on the side of the cells where the FIB beam hits the sample, ensuring the best protection.
source: Since the GIS needle was mounted at a similar angle as the FIB column, deposition of platinum occurred preferentially on the side of the cells where the FIB beam hits the sample, ensuring the best protection.
evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for the GIS needle positioning based on the geometry of the setup.

claim: A high-resolution (4096 × 3072 pixels, 35x magnification) overview image was taken with the SE2 detector for stage registration.
source: To calibrate stage registration a high-resolution (4096 × 3072 pixels, 35x magnification) overview image was taken with the SE2 detector, which provided the best information for identifying targets inside the vitrified ice and determining ice thickness.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging parameters used for stage registration.

claim: The overview image was registered by correlating three distinctive points on the image to their specific positions on the stage.
source: This overview image was then loaded onto the stage navigation bar and registered by correlating three distinctive points on the image to their specific positions on the stage as observed in the live SEM view.
evidence: This is a description of the stage registration procedure.

claim: For milling, patterns were defined to be executed using bi-directional and cross-section cycle mode with a 10 µm milling depth.
source: For milling, we defined the patterns to be executed using bi-directional and cross-section cycle mode with a 10 µm milling depth.
evidence: This is a description of the milling pattern parameters.

claim: The milling parameters (milling current, pattern size, milling depth, etc.) are adjustable on-the-fly to optimize each set of patterns for the target location and desired milling strategy.
source: It is important to note that the milling parameters (milling current, pattern size, milling depth, etc.) are adjustable on-the-fly to optimize each set of patterns for the target location and desired milling strategy.
evidence: This is a description of the flexibility of the method.

claim: To ensure successful milling during automation, it was essential to refine the stage location until the stage was able to perform targeting successfully.
source: To ensure successful milling during automation, it was essential to refine the stage location until the stage was able to perform targeting successfully.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the protocol development.

claim: Eight rectangular milling patterns were placed during testing: six rough milling and two polishing patterns.
source: When testing this methodology, we placed eight rectangular milling patterns: six rough milling and two polishing patterns (Table 3).
evidence: This is a description of the milling pattern configuration used in the study.

claim: The final polishing patterns were spaced 300 nm apart.
source: The final polishing patterns were spaced 300 nm apart, since we generally expected the generated lamellae to be thinner than the specified value.
evidence: This is a description of the polishing pattern spacing with rationale.

claim: It is possible to save milling patterns as a recipe, which can be dragged and dropped onto images of other milling targets to make uniform lamellae.
source: To make uniform lamellae, it was also possible to save these eight patterns as a recipe, which can be dragged and dropped onto images of other milling targets.

claim: In current lamella preparation workflows, samples are vitrified on transmission electron microscopy (TEM) grids by plunge-freezing.
source: In current lamella preparation workflows (Marko et al., 2007; Medeiros et al., 2018; Rigort et al., 2010; Strunk et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016), samples are vitrified on transmission electron microscopy (TEM) grids by plunge-freezing.
evidence: This is a description of standard practice in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: In current manual methods, rough milling uses a series of steps with decreasing FIB milling currents (e.g. 700 to 100 pA).
source: Using a series of 'rough milling' steps, sections above and below the desired lamella are sequentially removed by reducing the separation between two milling areas and using decreasing FIB milling currents (e.g. 700 to 100 pA) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is a description of the manual milling workflow with supporting figure.

claim: Once the lamella is thinned to ~500 nm by rough milling, additional targets are identified and thinned by rough milling in the same manner.
source: Once the lamella is thinned to ~500 nm, additional targets are identified and thinned by rough milling in the same manner.
evidence: This is a description of the manual workflow.

claim: To generate lamellae with a final thickness of 100–250 nm, the user returns to each target location and thins ('polishes') each lamella using a low (e.g. ≤50 pA) current.
source: To generate lamellae with a final thickness of 100–250 nm, the user returns to each target location and thins ('polishes') each lamella using a low (e.g. ≤50 pA) current (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a description of the manual polishing step with supporting figure.

claim: Previous manual milling methods used a real-time view to visually determine the time that a FIB current needed to cut through the specimen by visual end point detection.
source: Previously, manual milling methods used a real-time view in order to visually determine the time that a FIB current needed to cut through the specimen by visual end point detection.
evidence: This is a description of the manual method that the automated approach replaces.

claim: In the automated approach, the exposure time is calculated by the software using a user-specified milling depth, milling current, pattern size and material type.
source: In our automated approach, the exposure time is calculated by the software using a user-specified milling depth, milling current, pattern size and material type.
evidence: This is a description of how the automated method differs from manual methods.

claim: The user can decide whether to perform polishing for all targets in a manual or automated manner.
source: Subsequently, the user can decide whether to perform polishing for all targets in a manual or automated manner (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a description of the flexibility of the method.

claim: The automation of polishing follows the same routine as rough milling.
source: The automation of polishing follows the same routine as described above.
evidence: This is a description of the polishing automation procedure.

claim: For each set of patterns during automated milling, the stage automatically moves to the target position and executes stage backlash correction.
source: For each set of patterns, the stage automatically moves to the target position and executes stage backlash correction.
evidence: This is a description of the automated workflow.

claim: Image shifts are determined between the drift correction image recorded during setup and a drift correction image recorded after arriving at the target location, and any existing shifts are compensated for using FIB beam shifts.
source: Next, image shifts are determined between the drift correction image that was recorded during the setup procedure and a drift correction image that is recorded after arriving at the target location. Any existing shifts are compensated for, using FIB beam shifts, to achieve precise milling at the target location.
evidence: This is a description of the drift correction mechanism in the automated workflow.

claim: The rough milling patterns are exposed from the highest to the lowest current during automated milling.
source: The rough milling patterns are then exposed, from the highest to the lowest current.
evidence: This is a description of the milling sequence in the automated workflow.

claim: It is advisable to execute rough milling and polishing in quick succession.
source: Therefore, we find it advisable to execute rough milling and polishing in quick succession.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the observation that delays led to lamella bending and reduced success rates.

claim: A microtubule observed in a yeast tomogram had 13 protofilaments.
source: From a single slice through the tomogram it is possible to identify 13 protofilaments that make up the microtubule.
